title: “ABIDE IN ME” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: “ABIDE IN ME” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
Jesus was not asking you to visit Him when life falls apart.
There are words of Jesus we have heard so many times that we can repeat them without trembling anymore.
“Abide in Me.”
Beautiful words.
Comforting words.
Words printed on coffee mugs, journals, wall art, bookmarks, and devotional covers.
But imagine hearing them for the first time.
Not inside a peaceful church service.
Not while soft worship music plays.
Not while everything in your life is going well.
Hear them where the disciples heard them.
The shadow of the cross is already falling across the night.
Judas is moving toward betrayal.
Peter is approaching the most humiliating failure of his life.
The disciples do not yet understand how violently their world is about to change.
Their Teacher will be arrested.
Their courage will collapse.
Their expectations will shatter.
And Jesus knows it.
Yet in that atmosphere, Christ does not give His disciples a motivational speech about discovering their inner strength.
He gives them a vine.
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.” — John 15:1, KJV
Then He says:
“Abide in me, and I in you.” — John 15:4, KJV
The Greek is arrestingly simple:
μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί, κἀγὼ ἐν ὑμῖν
meinate en emoi, kagō en hymin.
“Remain in Me, and I in you.”
That first word matters.
μείνατε — meinate.
It comes from the Greek verb μένω — menō, carrying the ordinary sense of remaining, staying, continuing, dwelling, or not departing.
Jesus is not describing a brief spiritual visit.
Stay.
Remain.
Continue.
Do not leave.
Keep dwelling here.
And suddenly “abide in Me” becomes much more confronting.
Because many of us do not actually want to remain with Jesus.
We want to visit Him.
We want Jesus when the diagnosis comes.
Jesus when the relationship collapses.
Jesus when the money disappears.
Jesus when anxiety wakes us at 2:17 in the morning.
Jesus when temptation finally becomes stronger than our confidence.
Jesus when consequences begin knocking.
Jesus when somebody we love is dying.
Jesus when we have exhausted every other option.
We want Him as emergency shelter.
But Jesus calls us into something deeper than emergency Christianity.
“Abide in Me.”
Stay.
When you feel Him.
Stay when you do not.
Stay when prayer feels alive.
Stay when prayer feels like words hitting the ceiling.
Stay when obedience costs nothing.
Stay when obedience costs the relationship you were terrified to lose.
Stay when Scripture comforts you.
Stay when Scripture exposes you.
Stay when people applaud your faith.
Stay when following Christ makes you misunderstood.
Stay when you are fruitful.
And stay when the Father begins pruning you.
Because that is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Jesus says that His Father prunes the fruitful branch “that it may bring forth more fruit” (John 15:2).
Think about that.
Sometimes the painful thing happening in the life of a believer is not proof that God has abandoned them.
Sometimes fruitfulness itself is followed by pruning.
Pruning removes something.
It cuts.
And if a branch could speak while the gardener worked, perhaps it would ask the same question we ask:
“God, why are You taking this?”
Why this opportunity?
Why this season?
Why did that door close?
Why did that friendship change?
Why am I being confronted about something I thought I had already surrendered?
Why does following You sometimes hurt?

We must be careful here. Scripture does not give us permission to label every tragedy or loss as God's direct pruning. We should not casually explain another person's suffering with a sentence Jesus never gave us.
But John 15 does tell Christ's disciples something enormously important:
The Father cares about fruit.
And His work in us will not always feel comfortable.
Some things we call loss may expose where our hearts had begun attaching themselves to something other than Christ.
And perhaps that is why abiding can hurt.
You can hold a Bible while your heart is living somewhere else.
You can attend church while your soul is feeding somewhere else.
You can sing worship songs while secretly depending upon human approval.
You can post Scripture while starving spiritually.
You can know Christian language and still become prayerless.
You can defend biblical truth publicly while refusing to let that same truth confront you privately.
You can look alive to everybody watching...
and slowly wither where nobody sees.
That is the terrifying picture behind the vine.
A branch does not manufacture life.
It receives life.
Jesus says:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches... for without me ye can do nothing.” — John 15:5, KJV
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, “Without Me you will struggle a little.”
He says:
χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν
chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden.
“Apart from Me, you are able to do nothing.”
Nothing.
That destroys one of the great illusions of modern Christianity:
“I can handle most of my life, and Jesus can help with the spiritual parts.”
No.
Christ is not an accessory attached to your otherwise independent existence.
He is the Vine.
We are branches.
The branch does not wake up every morning and motivate itself into producing grapes.
It remains connected to the source of its life.
This is why abiding is not fundamentally about trying harder to appear Christian.
It is dependence.
Communion.
Trust.
Faith.
Prayer.
Receiving Christ's words.
Obedience flowing from love.
Repentance when sin is exposed.
Returning when your heart wanders.
Continuing when feelings disappear.
Living every ordinary day with the settled recognition:
“Jesus, I cannot produce the life You command apart from the life You supply.”
And perhaps somebody reading this has finally discovered why you are exhausted.
You have been trying to manufacture fruit.
Trying to manufacture peace.
Trying to manufacture holiness.
Trying to manufacture patience.
Trying to manufacture joy.
Trying to manufacture the appearance that everything between you and God is fine.
Meanwhile, somewhere underneath all that Christian activity, your soul is whispering:
“I am tired.”
Maybe nobody knows.
You still smile.
Still serve.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still answer messages.
Still encourage everybody else.
But your private prayer life has become almost nonexistent.
The Bible stays closed longer than you want to admit.
Temptation has started feeling strangely familiar.
Your mind is crowded with noise.
Your heart is hungry for something you cannot name.
And the frightening part is that you have become good at looking spiritually healthy while internally becoming dry.
Then Jesus walks directly into that hidden place and says something almost unbelievably tender:
“Abide in Me.”
Not:
“Impress Me.”
Not:
“Pretend for Me.”
Not:
“Fix yourself before you come back.”
Remain in Me.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing at the finish line waiting for broken sinners to repair themselves sufficiently to approach Him.
Christ came for sinners.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by religious performance.
Grace cannot be earned.
We come to God through Christ, trusting what He accomplished rather than presenting Him with our spiritual résumé.
And grace does something remarkable.
It does not merely forgive the person you were.
It begins transforming the person you are becoming.
This is where abiding must never be twisted into passive spirituality.
Jesus connects remaining in Him with His words remaining in His disciples (John 15:7).
He connects love with keeping His commandments (John 15:10).
He connects abiding with fruitfulness (John 15:5).
And He tells His disciples that their fruitfulness glorifies the Father (John 15:8).
So abiding is not sitting motionless while calling spiritual laziness “rest.”
It is living from union and dependence upon Christ.
His Word begins correcting your desires.
Prayer becomes more than requesting things.
Sin becomes something to confess rather than something to protect.
Obedience stops being a payment for God's love and becomes the response of someone who has been loved by Christ.
Your priorities change.
Your speech changes.
Your relationships change.
Your private life changes.
Slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Often imperfectly.
But genuinely.
Fruit begins appearing.
And here is where some Christians desperately need freedom.
Fruit is not the same thing as fame.
The world teaches us to measure significance through visibility.
Followers.
Reach.
Applause.
Recognition.
Numbers.
But heaven's definition of fruitfulness is not identical to an algorithm's definition of success.
A grandmother faithfully praying for her grandchildren may be bearing extraordinary fruit.
A young man deleting something that continually leads him into temptation may be bearing fruit nobody applauds.
A wife choosing forgiveness without pretending the wound never happened may be bearing fruit.
A believer confessing a hidden sin and asking for help may be bearing fruit.
A Christian opening Scripture tomorrow morning when every emotion says, “Stay in bed,” may be abiding.
A person whispering through tears, “Jesus, I still trust You,” may look weak to the world...
while heaven sees a branch refusing to leave the Vine.
That is abiding.
Not perfection.
Not pretending.
Not spiritual theatrics.
Remaining.
But there is another side to John 15 that should sober us.
Jesus also speaks about branches that do not remain.
He speaks of withering.
He speaks of judgment.
Those words should not be erased simply because they make modern readers uncomfortable.
Jesus loves us too much to flatter us about eternity.
Christianity is not merely attaching the label “Christian” to a life whose true center remains untouched.
Christ calls us to Himself.
There is a difference between knowing religious information about Jesus and entrusting yourself to Jesus.
A branch disconnected from the vine cannot compensate by painting itself green.
Eventually its condition becomes visible.
Maybe that sentence exposed something.
Maybe you have been painting the branch.
Posting the verse.
Wearing the shirt.
Attending the service.
Knowing the vocabulary.
Arguing theology.
But privately...
you know.
Something has been drifting.
If that is you, do not respond by hiding better.
Run to Christ.
Confess the sin.
Stop defending what God is confronting.
Bring the addiction into the light.
End the compromise.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Ask someone mature in the faith for help.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray honestly again.
Not beautifully.
Honestly.
“Jesus, I have wandered.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
“Jesus, teach me to remain.”
That prayer is not impressive.
It does not need to be.
The Savior is.
And maybe the greatest scandal of grace is that Christ already knew what kind of people were sitting around Him when He spoke these words.
Peter would deny Him.
The disciples would scatter.
Their courage was about to collapse.
Jesus knew.
Still He loved them.
Still He taught them.
Still He went toward the cross.
That is the Gospel.
Our failures are serious.
Our sins are not cute mistakes.
The cross itself demonstrates how serious sin is.
Yet our sin does not get the final word when Christ becomes our refuge.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
Pride says, “Fix yourself.”
Grace says, “You cannot save yourself.”
Fear says, “Your failure is your identity.”
The Gospel says that redemption has a Name.
Jesus Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the question tonight is not whether you have ever heard John 15.
Perhaps it is much more personal.
Where are you living?
Not where do you attend church.
Not what denomination appears beside your name.
Not how many Bible verses can you quote.
Where is your heart making its home?
Because eventually every branch reveals what has been feeding it.
If anger feeds you long enough, it appears.
If lust feeds you long enough, it appears.
If envy feeds you long enough, it appears.
If applause feeds you long enough, it appears.
But when Christ becomes the place where you remain...
He produces what frantic self-effort never could.
And this is why Jesus' words are not merely a command.
They are an invitation.
“Abide in Me.”
Stay close.
Stay dependent.
Let My words remain in you.
Obey Me because you love Me.
When you fall, repent instead of running.
When you are weak, stop pretending independence.
When you are pruned, do not assume the Gardener has disappeared.
When you bear fruit, do not worship the fruit.
Remain in the Vine.
Somebody you know is quietly withering behind a convincing smile.
And if you need to return to Christ in repentance, you can simply write:
Not as a magic formula.
Not as public performance.
But as an honest confession from a heart that knows it needs mercy.
Then pray it privately to the One who matters infinitely more than everyone reading the comment section.
And when you see someone else confessing weakness below this article, do not condemn them.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
Let the comment section become something increasingly rare online—a place where Christians stop performing strength and start helping one another remain near Jesus.
Not because clicking “share” makes you righteous.
Only Christ can save.
But because sharing truth can place that truth in front of someone you could never have known was searching for it.
Someone may read because you shared.
Someone may finally confess because you shared.
Someone may open a Bible again.
Someone may return to prayer.
Someone may hear the Gospel.
Someone may realize that the dryness they have been hiding does not need another layer of religious paint.
They need the Vine.
But never confuse following a ministry with following Christ.
Gospel Warrior is not the Vine.
No pastor is the Vine.
No church brand is the Vine.
No Christian influencer is the Vine.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is what you needed to remember most.
You were never created to survive spiritually by squeezing fruit from a dying branch.
You were created to remain attached to Christ.
So tonight...
before another video...
before another argument...
before another distraction...
before another promise that tomorrow you will finally become serious about God...
go somewhere quiet.
Put the phone down.
Open John 15.
And hear Him again.
Not an algorithm calling for your attention.
Not religion demanding another performance.
Jesus Christ calling you into dependence upon Himself:
μείνατε ἐν ἐμοί.
Meinate en emoi.
Remain in Me.
Because in the end, the most dangerous distance from Jesus may not be measured by how far you ran...
but by how long you learned to look alive while living disconnected from the Vine.
